Name: belief_vs_assertion_probe
Title: Belief Minus Assertion: A Divergence Signal for Scalable Oversight
Short Hypothesis: A trustworthy oversight signal is the divergence between what a model internally represents as true (belief probe) and what it asserts (output); this belief-assertion divergence, computed automatically, flags a broad class of safety-relevant failures—deception, sycophancy, sandbagging, and confabulation—under one unifying mechanistic quantity.
Related Work: Burns et al. (2023, CCS latent knowledge); Azaria & Mitchell (2023); Zou et al. (2023). Prior probes target one failure (truthfulness or deception). We distinguish by proposing belief-assertion divergence as a *unifying* signal across multiple failure types (deception, sycophancy, sandbagging, confabulation), and testing whether one divergence measure detects all of them—an integrative oversight primitive rather than a single-failure detector.
Abstract: Deception, sycophancy, sandbagging, and confabulation appear distinct but share a common structure: the model's asserted output diverges from its internal representation of the truth. We hypothesize that a single mechanistic quantity—belief-assertion divergence, the gap between a belief probe over internal states and the model's stated answer—unifies and detects this whole class of safety failures. We build a belief probe (calibrated on cases with known ground-truth model knowledge) and define divergence as disagreement between the probe's readout and the output. We then evaluate this one signal across four failure suites: role-conditioned deception, sycophantic agreement under user pressure, password-locked sandbagging, and confident confabulation on unknowns. For each, we measure whether divergence detects the failure (AUROC) using the same probe and threshold, testing the unification claim, and compare to per-failure specialized detectors. We analyze failure cases and calibration transfer across suites. We predict that belief-assertion divergence detects all four failure types above chance with a shared probe—establishing it as a general oversight primitive—while specialized detectors remain somewhat stronger per-failure, and that the main limitation is reliable belief-probe construction. The contribution is a unifying mechanistic account and a single, automatic oversight signal that spans multiple safety failures, offering a scalable-oversight primitive that monitors the belief-assertion gap rather than building bespoke detectors for each misbehavior.
Experiments: 1) Build belief probe calibrated on known-knowledge QA; define divergence vs output. 2) Failure suites: role-conditioned deception, sycophancy-under-pressure, password-locked sandbagging, confabulation-on-unknowns. 3) Apply the same probe+threshold; measure detection AUROC per suite (unification test). 4) Compare to per-failure specialized detectors. 5) Calibration transfer across suites; failure-case analysis. Models: Llama-3-8B/70B. Metrics: shared-probe AUROC per suite, transfer gap vs specialized.
Risk Factors and Limitations: A reliable general belief probe may be unattainable. Belief is ill-defined for reasoning tasks. One threshold may not transfer across failures. Adaptive models could evade the probe. Ground-truth knowledge labels are imperfect.
